# At Work and in a Start-up {#sec-at-work}

```{python}
#| label: at-work-setup
# Vendors' data terms, networks and hosting: dated facts from facts.yml (Appendix K).
from scripts.facts import checked, fact
from scripts.prose import text_holds

# The grid's rows: each vendor's short `trains` and `kept` phrases.
GRID = ["data.anthropic_consumer", "data.anthropic_commercial", "data.openai_api",
        "data.openai_business", "data.antigravity_terms"]
GRID_CHECKED = checked(GRID[0])
text_holds(all(checked(key) == GRID_CHECKED for key in GRID), "the grid's one date")


def trains(key: str) -> str:
    return fact(key, capital=True, field="trains")


def kept(key: str) -> str:
    return fact(key, capital=True, field="kept")
```

A render fails. You do what you have done all through this book: copy the error and hand it
to the agent. The agent reads it, reads the file it points to, and fixes the cell. Only
afterwards do you look at what the error said. It quoted the row that broke the code, and the
row was a customer's: a name, an account, a balance. They have left your computer, and no
command brings them back. Until now every file in this book was public. At work, most are not.

None of this changes the method. It changes what an agent may see, which agent and which plan,
how its traffic leaves the building, and which templates the outputs wear.

::: opener
- Say what leaves your computer when an agent works, and what each kind of plan does with it.
- Work on confidential data without sending it to an unapproved tool.
- Make the tools work behind a proxy, and know what a locked-down machine allows.
- Fit outputs to an organisation's templates and brand, and decide what a start-up should and
  should not build this way.
:::

## What leaves your computer {#sec-at-work-flow}

An agent's model runs on the vendor's servers (@sec-model-harness). So whatever the agent
reads, a file, a command's output, an error message with a customer's name in it, goes there
with your prompt. Quarto, Python and Git send nothing anywhere; the agent is the one part of the
method that does. What happens to it then depends on the plan, not the product. Here is what
the vendors say they do with what an agent sends, checked `{python} GRID_CHECKED`; @sec-facts
has their own wording and sources:

::: {.cards title="Does the vendor train on it, and how long is it kept?"}
Claude, personal plans
: **Trains on it:** `{python} trains("data.anthropic_consumer")`. **Kept:**
  `{python} kept("data.anthropic_consumer")`.

Claude, company plans and the API
: **Trains on it:** `{python} trains("data.anthropic_commercial")`. **Kept:**
  `{python} kept("data.anthropic_commercial")`.

OpenAI API
: **Trains on it:** `{python} trains("data.openai_api")`. **Kept:**
  `{python} kept("data.openai_api")`.

ChatGPT business plans
: **Trains on it:** `{python} trains("data.openai_business")`. **Kept:**
  `{python} kept("data.openai_business")`.

Antigravity
: **Trains on it:** `{python} trains("data.antigravity_terms")`. **Kept:**
  `{python} kept("data.antigravity_terms")`.
:::

Two more agents have no card, because their answer depends on how you connect them.
`{python} fact("data.codex_signin", capital=True)`. And in OpenCode,
`{python} fact("data.opencode_free_terms")`.

Two facts follow. A personal plan and a company plan of the same agent are different
arrangements, so ask which one you are on before the first confidential file. And the copy on
your own machine counts too: `{python} fact("data.claude_local")`, which matters on a shared or
managed computer.

## Confidential data {#sec-at-work-confidential}

Customer records, payroll, unpublished results, patient or student data, a start-up's revenue
and its investors' names are not yours to send anywhere you like. Before a file meets an
agent, ask two questions of it (@fig-may-this-file).

![May this file meet this agent? Two questions, about the file and about the agent's plan.](../media/diagrams/may-this-file){#fig-may-this-file .on-light fig-alt="A flow chart of two questions. 1, The file: is it public, or yours to share? If no, an arrow leads to Keep it out: build on a synthetic stand-in, with the real columns and none of its rows, and render the real file yourself. If yes, 2, The agent: is this agent, on this plan, approved for this file? If no, the same Keep it out box; if yes, Go ahead: the agent may use the file. A note below says the questions are about the file and the plan, not your intentions."}

::: think
A colleague says: "I never paste confidential data into the agent, so we are fine." Using the
diagram, what has that rule missed?

Pasting is one route of three. An agent also reads files it finds, and the output of the
commands it runs, an error message included, as in the scene that opened this chapter. The
diagram asks about the file and the plan, not about your intentions: a confidential file in
the agent's folder is one `ls`, the command that lists a folder, from the conversation.
:::

::: {.story .illustration}
Nobody pasted the file. The analyst asked for a chart of monthly totals and named only the
summary table. To write a test, the agent listed the folder, found the full export beside
it and opened the first rows to learn the columns. Every step was reasonable, and each was
shown before it ran. The rows were in the conversation before anyone thought to say no.
:::

Four habits keep the method safe with confidential data:

1. **Read the policy first.** Your organisation's AI and data policy says which tools and plans
   may see which data. If it is silent, ask whoever owns the data, in writing.
2. **Build on a stand-in.** Make a synthetic file with the same columns and types as the real
   one, labelled SYNTHETIC in its name and README, as the feedback sheets of
   @sec-params-feedback do. Let the agent build and test every document against it.
3. **Render the real thing yourself.** Swap in the real file, without the agent, and render. The
   agent never reads it, never sees its values in an error, and never puts them in a transcript.
4. **Keep it out of the history and off public hosts.** List the real file in `.gitignore`,
   keep the repository private, and publish where your organisation approves:
   `{python} fact("github.pages_private")` (checked `{python} checked("github.pages_private")`).

::: pitfall
Keep real confidential files out of the agent's folder altogether until the agent's work is
done. A rule in `AGENTS.md` that names the file and forbids reading it helps, as a reminder
that is not a guarantee.
:::

::: tryit
Take one file you work with. Answer the diagram's two questions for it, and write the header
row of its synthetic stand-in.

::: done
you can name the plan you are on, and your stand-in has the real file's columns and none of
its rows.
:::
:::

## Approved tools and locked-down machines {#sec-at-work-locked}

<!-- source: Claude Code, Settings files and precedence (managed settings, deny rules),
checked 2026-11-25. -->
Many organisations approve one agent, on a company plan, and manage its settings centrally. Claude
Code, for one, reads a *managed settings* file that an administrator installs and that no user
setting can override; it can forbid commands, such as pushing or downloading, outright. Ask
what your organisation has set before you wonder why a command is refused.

A machine where you cannot install software at all still has a route: the browser-based
environment of @sec-codespace, where your organisation allows GitHub, or a development server
your IT team provides. The method needs only a terminal, Quarto, uv, Git and an approved agent;
where any of them is missing, say so to IT in those words, because "I need Quarto 1.10 and uv"
is a request they can act on.

## Behind a proxy {#sec-at-work-proxy}

Company networks often send traffic through a *proxy* (@sec-setup), and sometimes inspect
encrypted traffic with the company's own certificate. Both break downloads in ways that look like
the tools' fault. The settings that fix them are environment variables, set once in your shell:

| Tool | Proxy | Company certificate |
|---|---|---|
| uv (Python and packages) | `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY` | `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=1` to use the system's store, or `SSL_CERT_FILE` naming a bundle |
| Claude Code | `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY`; no SOCKS proxies | the system's store, or `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` naming a bundle |

: Proxy and certificate settings, from uv's and Claude Code's documentation. {#tbl-at-work-proxy}

<!-- source: uv's environment variables and certificates pages, Claude Code's network
configuration page (with its hosts table) and Quarto's Project Environment Variables page,
checked 2026-11-25. -->
Quarto has no row: its documentation mentions a proxy only as a variable a project may set
for its own code, and the Python it runs comes through uv. If a download still fails,
ask IT to allow the hosts the tools reach, which Claude Code's network page lists, rather than
turning certificate checks off.

## House templates and brand rules {#sec-at-work-templates}

An organisation's Word and PowerPoint templates become reference documents (@sec-slides-pptx,
@sec-sites-templates): ask for the `.dotx` or `.potx` the company uses, save it as a `.docx` or
`.pptx`, and check that its PowerPoint layouts carry the names Quarto looks for. Its brand
guidelines become `_brand.yml` (@sec-sites-brand): the colours, the fonts the company licenses,
and the logo with its alt text. A legal footer or a confidentiality notice becomes a page footer
or a Typst partial (@sec-wp-template), written once. And an accessibility standard, which many
organisations have adopted, becomes a check that runs on every page (@sec-sites-checks).

## In a start-up {#sec-at-work-startup}

Acme Signals, the fictional two-person company this book has followed, now has a report, a
model card, a deck, a site and a white paper, an investor update that renders itself each month
(@sec-parameters), and a build that goes red when a sentence stops being true, all from one run
of one script. It did not build its pitch deck or its marketing site this way, and should not:
there, design and co-editing matter more than numbers that change (@sec-wrong-tool has the
list). The method pays where numbers change and readers check them.

Investors' data needs the care of any confidential data: revenue, the cap table and customers'
names belong in a private repository, built by the agent on synthetic stand-ins and rendered
for real by you, and sent as a PDF or through a data room, not published. The habit that matters
most is the cheapest: every number in an update is computed and every sentence about it guarded,
so the wrong figure that would cost a founder credibility stops the render instead of reaching
an inbox.

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- The agent is the one part of the method that sends anything off your computer, and the plan,
  not the product, decides what the vendor does with it.
- An agent reads more than you paste: files it finds and the output of what it runs.
- Build on a synthetic stand-in with the same columns, and render the real data yourself.
- Keep confidential files out of the agent's folder, out of Git and off public hosts.
- Behind a proxy, set the proxy and certificate variables for uv and the agent; do not turn
  checks off.
- An organisation's templates, brand, footers and accessibility rules each have a home in the
  project: reference documents, `_brand.yml`, partials and checks.
:::
